title: What kind of AI-made game would actually impress you?
author: ineedthealgorithm
selftext:
I’ve been seeing a lot of AI-generated games lately. And lot of them are starting to feel pretty similar.

Same kinds of mechanics, same look, same “quick demo” vibe.

So I’m curious — what kind of game would actually impress you if it was made with AI?

Not just something that works, but something you’d actually want to play.

Is it more about originality, deeper mechanics, better feel, or something else?

comments.author: TheeJestersCurse

replies.author: TransmissionEngPM
replies.body:
I've tried to go down this road multiple times, and it just kind of spiral's out of control with massive context windows, DB's etc. I'm sure someone is going to crack it at some point but my vision was always something like WoW, but all of the NPC's can interact within their domain, questlines are more of a unique adventure/character etc. So you end up at the same place in the end, but it's much more immersive than canned quest text.

I built something along these lines for my kids, it's a daily adventure book, uses claude to run a chron, generates a daily "Escape Room", nano bana generates the imagery for the story, and then the story/escape adventure is guided, but also not locked. It's like reading 2.0, some interaction with the overall story and they're participating. Maybe someday I can evolve it from there, but kids seem to really like it!

replies.author: Simicy
replies.body:
I may be working on something of interest to you - an sdk/plugin for creating pipelines for generative content. The main focus was npc dialogue but the architecture is adaptable enough to do other things. Have a friend making a monster battler with it so he can command them verbally, im working on an interactive drama. 

Goal was to use regression models and RAG together to focus NPC/scene/context configs and game context down to bite sized system prompts for local LLMs (using qwen 3.5 4B atm) - so the final system prompt is closer to stage directions than an open ended prompt so that behavior can be kept more consistent/predictable and avoid drift. 

Once you settle on the pre and post-processing handlers you like in a given pipeline, it then lets you export training schemas for the regression models/LoRA training for even further refinement of the models you selected. 

Just finished a massive rewrite of the codebase because the only language ive used professionally is clojure, and i took for granted how much I relied on immutable data which bit me in the butt when I swapped to python for all the ML libraries. But now ive got everything wrapped in padded cells of enforced contracts so I can finally move back to A/B testing different methods for improving npc dialogue and writing more handlers.

Registered the package as conjured on pypi but it still needs a bit of work before i update that with the actual sdk

replies.author: TheeJestersCurse
replies.body:
generally the idea is working with less direct inputs instead of clogging the context window directly. less generating dialogue so much as generating responses to stimuli if that makes sense? like a player discovers or interacts with something, and an npc responds in some way by reading the world state or player action and selecting the closest relevant line of dialogue.

i think the big thing is i'd prioritize an experience that can be installed on device instead of relying on cloud models that you have to buy credits for, which may limit context (although this could change if that new architecture is adopted).

comments.author: void--null
comments.body:
The thing that would impress me is complexity. If you understand the systems well enough to actually direct the AI instead of letting it drive, the result speaks for itself regardless of how it was made. 

The problem is most people don't have deep knowledge of system design and can't wrap their head around a lot of the higher level concepts in programming. So they let the AI take more of the wheel, they don't catch the mistakes, and the games stay low complexity to compensate. 

The impressive AI game is going to come from someone who already knew how to build it and used AI to get there faster, not from someone who needed AI to build it at all.

comments.author: fantasstic_bet
comments.body:
Utilizing AI to enhance immersion and offer more emergent gameplay in a very significant way would impress me. Using AI for generative content isn’t impressive as it pushes games l/media closer to a a visual average that makes the game harder to distinguish from its peers. Using it for specific character interactions, though? That could be awesome to see more of.

As someone who works in advertising and marketing for games and has been in the industry for the last decade, the glow from generative AI content has evaporated. Now, it’s seen as a tool that pushes your game closer to an “average” state. You’ll find that especially with generative AI for art that the models will fight you when you try and steer them away from the average center.
